input.title: An allow on execute confers read of that scope, so an administration grant should name scope 'auth' rather than '*'

input.description: Executing means reading the state it applies to. The converse does not hold, a deny on execute says nothing about read, and reads ignore the operation list; execute on '*' publishes all scopes.

input.content:
Executing an operation means reading the state it applies to, so `covers` was extended: a read request is covered by a grant that **allows execute** on the same scope, as well as by an explicit read grant.

```
covers(grant, request):
   scopeReaches(grant.capability.scope, request.scope)
   and ( <the verb the grant names>
      or (request.verb == "read" and grant.effect == "allow" and grant.capability.can == "execute") )
```

Two exclusions keep the implication from reaching further:

- A **deny on execute withholds the write and says nothing about the read** — otherwise a policy locking writes down would silently revoke a read grant standing before it.
- The **`operation` list is not consulted for a read**. It restricts which operations may be executed, not whether the scope is visible; consulting it would mean a narrowed execute grant conferred *less* read than a broad one. The `scoped-reads` recipe shows Alice, whose only grant names a single operation, reading the whole `global` scope — and Carol, who holds a read grant, reading the expenses and still unable to submit one.

This makes the **shape of an administration grant matter**. `{ can: "execute", scope: "*" }` now also serves every domain scope of the document to whoever it names. A policy that means "administration stays reachable" should name the `auth` scope, which is all the retention rule requires; the spec's worked toll example dropped its separate `g-admin-read` grant for exactly this reason, and the `scoped-reads` recipe scopes every administration grant to `auth` while noting that `document-acl`, `revocation-race` and `group-principals` still use `*`.
